questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has passed bright red urine three times over 2 weeks. She has no pain, fever or dysuria. She has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painless visible haematuria in an older smoker is bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinoma) until proven otherwise.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years
steps.x: Painless, visible, recurrent haematuria plus heavy smoking.

elim: Cystitis causes dysuria and frequency; her haematuria is painless with no urinary symptoms.
She has no fever or loin pain.
Stones cause severe colicky loin pain.
A caruncle causes spotting from the urethral meatus, not repeated frank haematuria in a heavy smoker.

steps.x: B. Bladder cancer. Painless haematuria + smoker = bladder cancer until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has 3 months of frequency, urgency and burning when passing urine. Three urine cultures have been negative and two courses of antibiotics have not helped. steps.x: B. Carcinoma in situ of the bladder. Sterile 'cystitis' with haematuria in a smoker: think CIS of the bladder.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man spent 30 years working in a factory making fabric dyes. He now has painless visible haematuria. Flexible cystoscopy shows a papillary tumour on the bladder wall, which is biopsied. He has never travelled outside Europe and has never had a catheter.

Occupational dye exposure; the SCC risk factors are excluded.

elim: Bladder adenocarcinoma is rare and linked to urachal remnants.

This is very rare in the bladder.

steps.x: E. Transitional cell carcinoma. Dyes, rubber, smoking: transitional cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman who grew up in Malawi has painless haematuria. As a child she often swam in Lake Malawi and passed blood in her urine. She has never smoked. Cystoscopy shows a solid tumour in the bladder wall with surrounding thickened, chalky mucosa, which is biopsied.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has painless visible haematuria. Ten years ago she had a course of oral cyclophosphamide for granulomatosis with polyangiitis, now in remission on azathioprine. She has never smoked or had a catheter. She also takes ramipril and omeprazole.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with muscle-invasive transitional cell carcinoma near both ureteric orifices has 1 week of reduced urine output and nausea. He has no pain. His bladder is not palpable after catheterisation. Ultrasound has been requested.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had a radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer 18 months ago. He now has 6 weeks of constant pain in his lower back that wakes him at night. There is tenderness over L2. His calcium is raised and ALP is raised.

questions.q: Which is the most important prognostic factor?

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has painless visible haematuria. He worked as an accountant, drinks 10 units of alcohol a week, has smoked 30 cigarettes a day since he was 18, has type 2 diabetes and drinks four cups of coffee a day. He has never had a catheter.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for his likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Smoking is the most important risk factor for bladder (transitional cell) cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important risk factor for his likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

steps.x: Painless haematuria and a long, heavy smoking history.

elim: Alcohol is not a significant bladder cancer risk factor.

Diabetes is not a major bladder cancer risk factor.

steps.x: D. Smoking. Smoking is the biggest risk factor for bladder cancer.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with atrial fibrillation on apixaban has passed red urine twice in a week. She has no pain or urinary symptoms. Her blood count and renal function are normal. Her GP says the anticoagulant is the likely cause and plans no investigation. She is an ex-smoker.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Painless visible haematuria in an anticoagulated older ex-smoker must be investigated for bladder cancer; anticoagulants unmask lesions rather than cause bleeding de novo.

Painless visible haematuria; the anticoagulant does not explain it away.

No pain.
She has no urinary symptoms.

steps.x: B. Bladder cancer. Never blame the anticoagulant: investigate painless haematuria.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man notices his urine is pink at the start of the day, on and off over a month. He has no pain, frequency or weight loss. He worked in a rubber tyre factory for 25 years. His observations are normal and his prostate feels benign on examination.

o: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder

steps.x: Intermittent painless haematuria and occupational aromatic amines.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man tells his GP that his urine looked red once last week. He had eaten beetroot that day, but his wife is worried. He has no pain or urinary symptoms. He smokes. His temperature is 36.6°C and his abdomen is soft and non-tender.

questions.e: First confirm haematuria with urinalysis and urine microscopy, which also excludes infection and pigments such as beetroot.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with painless visible haematuria has had a CT urogram, which shows a 2 cm filling defect on the left lateral wall of the bladder. The upper urinary tracts are normal. He is an ex-smoker with no other medical problems.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has painless visible haematuria. She is a heavy smoker. Flexible cystoscopy shows normal bladder mucosa with no tumour. Her urine culture is negative and renal function is normal. Her blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg and she takes no anticoagulants.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has a large bladder tumour on cystoscopy. Biopsy shows high-grade transitional cell carcinoma invading the detrusor muscle. He is fit and keen on curative treatment. The team needs to know whether there is spread outside the bladder.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with untreated bladder cancer awaiting surgery comes to the emergency department. She has passed large clots for a day and now cannot pass urine. Her lower abdomen is tender and dull to percussion up to the umbilicus. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg.
